Art foundation NODE told WIRED the robots were taken out on a walk to promote Beeple’s upcoming exhibition in Palo Alto. Original Video Credit: IG/robotstory.ae Packed tightly inside its transport case, the humanoid robot begins unfolding its articulated limbs before extending both feet onto the floor. It then raises its torso, positions itself on the edge of the case, and transitions into a full standing posture without being physically lifted by a person. Coordinated electric joints and onboard control systems manage the sequence by continuously controlling limb positions and balance as the robot shifts its weight. Its arms and legs work together to create stable points of support while the body moves from a folded position to standing. Self-deployment demonstrates how humanoid robots can perform more than programmed walking or manipulation tasks. Being able to transition between complex body positions with minimal human assistance could make these machines easier to transport, deploy, and operate in real-world environments. XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. Robot plays "The Butterfly Lovers" on the erhu | 二胡 | 梁祝 | 乐器 The Erhu is a traditional Chinese bowed string instrument. It originated in the Tang Dynasty, with its predecessor being the "Xiqin" played by northern ethnic minorities. Although its structure is simple — a wooden sound box covered with python skin at the front, a neck standing upright on it, and two strings sounded by a bow — it possesses great acoustic wisdom. The timbre of the Erhu closely resembles the human voice, capable of vividly expressing emotions such as joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness.#robot #robotics #erhu #music #future

Industrial humanoid robots are looking less humanlike every day.  The Chinese company LimX Dynamics just shared footage of its TRON 2 dual-arm robot integrated with an industrial robotic arm. The TRON 2 multi-form-factor robot has gone viral in the past for its modular design that can transform into a humanoid, a quadruped, or even be combined into a centaur.    In the industrial setup, TRON 2 is mounted onto a traditional robotic arm to extend its reach. It uses a custom attachment to hold and operate a power drill and nailer to assemble wooden frames and panels. It then applies spray finishing.    The TRON 2 is priced starting around $7,000 in China but international pricing begins around $13,000.   Shenzhen-based LimX is scaling production of its TRON platform, along with its full-sized humanoid robot Oli, and its sister, Luna, after securing around $400 million so far in 2026. Valued at $2.2 billion, it's one of many Chinese robotics startups racing toward a public listing. #robotics #robot #industrialrobot #ai #automation
